title: Encryption
objective: After this level you can explain how encryption keeps messages private.
summary: Encryption uses a key to turn plaintext into ciphertext. Diffie and Hellman's 1976 public-key idea lets strangers keep secrets: one key locks, another unlocks.

cards.headline: Your messages pass through networks you'll never see.
cards.body: Remember Level 62? Your packets travel over whatever route is available, across many connected networks. So what keeps the computers along the way from reading your bank details? The packets are scrambled, and only the intended recipient can unscramble them.

cards.headline: Scramble it with a key
cards.body: Encryption uses a method and a key to turn readable plaintext into scrambled ciphertext, so only someone with the right key can read it. Julius Caesar used a simple version: he replaced each letter with the one three places down the alphabet, so HELLO became KHOOR. His key was the number three. It's also easy to crack, because there are only 25 possible shifts to try.

cards.headline: The first-secret problem
cards.body: A shared key has a catch: both sides need it before they can talk privately, and you've never met your bank's computers. How do you agree on a key when anyone might be listening? In 1976, Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published a blueprint for communicating over an open channel, with no prearrangement, while keeping messages secret from eavesdroppers.

cards.fact: Public-key encryption uses two keys: one locks, and a different one unlocks.
cards.context: Picture handing out open padlocks: anyone can snap one shut on a box, but only you hold the key that opens it. Public-key cryptography became the backbone of modern internet security, and it lets your browser check that your bank is really who it claims to be. The padlock icon beside a web address signals that your traffic to that site is encrypted.

cards.headline: Encryption: unlocked
learned: Encryption turns plaintext into ciphertext using a key
Caesar shifted letters three places; it's easy to break
Diffie and Hellman (1976): secrets with no prearranged key
Public-key encryption: one key locks, a different key unlocks

questions.prompt: In encryption, what does a key turn readable plaintext into?

options.label: Ciphertext only the right key can read
A shorter file that loads faster
options.rationale: Encryption hides meaning; it isn't about size.

questions.explanation: Encryption turns plaintext into ciphertext; only someone with the right key can turn it back.

questions.prompt: What problem did Diffie and Hellman's 1976 blueprint solve?

options.label: Keeping messages secret with no key agreed in advance
Making messages travel faster across the network
options.rationale: Speed wasn't the goal; secrecy was.

questions.explanation: Their blueprint let people communicate over an open channel with no prearrangement and still keep their messages secret.

questions.prompt: Level 52's ASCII code turns letters into numbers. What makes encryption different from a code like that?

options.label: It turns each letter into a byte of 0s and 1s
options.rationale: That's ASCII encoding, which needs no key to read.

options.label: It shortens the text so it travels faster
options.rationale: Encryption scrambles text; it isn't about size or speed.

options.label: Only someone with the right key can read it
It sends the letters as radio waves
options.rationale: That's how Wi-Fi carries data, not what encryption does.

questions.explanation: Encryption uses a key to turn plaintext into ciphertext, so only the holder of the right key can read it.
